title: Are there games with primarily ai visual assets that have done well on steam?
author: RuinoftheReckless
selftext:
Not counting gacha style f2p phone games, etc...i have been looking througj steam for even one single 'indy game' that uses primarily ai genwrated visual assets and actually had a large number of sales or a large, engaged community.

I cant find even one. In fact most of the games i see on steam that disclose large amounts of ai gen assets have almost no sales or engagement at all.

This leads me to conclude either; the quality of ai assets is still not quite high enough to compete against human made visual design and assets, the quality of devs using the tech has not reached an acceptable level yet, it hasnt been long enough for a breakout success to emerge, or that the people that buy indy games see ai art and ai disclosures as a shorthand sign for low quality and they lose interest the moment they see it.

  
Are there any examples of big successes fueled by primarily ai gen visual assets?

replies.author: RuinoftheReckless
replies.body:
Yeah i'm going through list now and sorting by rating. 

\#1. Crime Scene Cleaner -> "*AI-generated art is NOT something we want to include in our game."*  
*#2. Take me, Vitaly -> Uses AI art extensively, looks like a pretty low quality 'sex game'*   
*#3 RetroMaze -> uses AI Art for steam community cards only.*   
*#4 Politics the Game -> AI sounds and music.*   
*#5 SubZero -> Two minutes of AI generated cinematics.*   
*#6  Stone Simulator -> AI localization used for translation.*   
*#7 Cyber Knights: Flashpoint -> Noo Ai Used except for translation.* 

*#8 Eventide Matter -> Ai used for a small amount of asset generation.*   
*#9 Island Survival -> AI use accounts for < 1% of art assets used.*   
*#10 Hidden Girls -> Sloppy 1.00 AI hentai game.  (first game on list that discloses extensive use of AI.)*   
\#11 Megastore Simulator -> Capsule images were AI generated. 

  
So yeah, the SteamDB listings here seem to confirm my suspicion rather than dispel it. All games listed here appear to fall into three basic categories: 

1. Games where the AI disclosure is that AI was not used. Or that it was used very minimally for only a specific thing (like a robot voice on one specific character.)   
2. Games that use a slightly larger amount of AI assets of one kind or another to fill in one specific gap. Usually music or voice.   
3. Extremely cheap (< 4.00 price tag) /low quality looking AI hentai games. 

  
I am unable to find a single game here that is; 

  
1. not hentai

2. discloses extensive ai use for visual assets and

3. has >100 reviews on Steam and an overall 'positive' rating (which is a REALLY low bar.)

comments.author: Varrianda
comments.body:
I really tried to make AI art work, but it’s really only good for concept art. You still need to be artistically skilled to make use of AI in its current state, and you likely wouldn’t make a post like this if you were. The art is just too inconsistent, the style drifts too hard, and it’s very bad at solid colors(if you zoom in on a solid blue, you’ll see 50 different slightly different shades of blue). I can’t speak for 3d, but I’d imagine the issues are similar. If you’re making a serious project, you’ll still likely need to commission art.

The only success I’ve had with AI art is prototyping, and for 8bit-32bit pixel art games. 32bit is still a bit dicey depending on what you’re making, but for really simple pixel art it’s fine. I’ve also had some luck using it with seed images/seed styles for prototyping(e.g. taking a bandit tent -> using it to create a goblin themed tent with a similar style).

replies.author: Alive-Shoulder-4042
replies.body:
To make it flawless: You have to be able to recreate  in a consistent style for every asset. Even if you did give the same context in a consistent style, there’s still going to be variance, especially with lighting.

If you’re aware of those problems and how to correct, you can build around it within your means. But it shouldn’t be producing anything beyond your skill level when it comes to assets.

replies.author: Varrianda
replies.body:
That’s my point though, AI art isn’t plug n’ play. It still takes effort to produce good assets. We’re not at the point yet where you can say “generate me a full tileset for my forest” and it just does it for you.

If you’re either not interested in art, or just bad at it, AI lets you slop something together.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: I can't speak for every dev... But I can say that while I've tried using AI Art in my work, any actual AI art use in game took longer to refine and match my style consistently than if I just created it from scratch myself. I do use it extensively for concept art, but then I create in my own style (flat color/ toon) because I don't have to worry about style drift at that point. Additionally, AI animations are a joke... So I animate my hand with Skeletal 2d animations, allowing me to reuse them with a variety of assets rather than having to go through a img -> vid process and then use  special tools to grab specific frames, at which point each frame would usually need extreme touch-ups due to motion blur artifacts intrinsic with AI video gens. That might still be a time saver if someone  didn't have customizable characters, or equipment, or whatever in their game.  But in one where you might have thousands of permutations of appearances for a skeleton, you'd have to then do animation sets for all X of those permutations, and it would be entirely unrealistic. So this immediately precludes using AI art/animation for games that require that kind of consistency and continuity -- or at least makes it a lot less worth it. There are probably a lot of people out there who COULD be using AI art, and maybe it'd even still save a bit of time, but if they're like me, it's a lot easier to just make the asset yourself, you then have layers already built and ready to animate, etc...   Compared to taking an  AI asset, touching it up into your style, layering it out for animation and filling in the gaps, etc. The former doesn't require me to disclose AI u se for art, since I'm not using it,  and takes the same or less time... Soooo I just do that. And then for my game world (which is low poly 3d), I just model that by hand or use asset packs, as AI   3d gen wastes a crap load of polys for no reason. And while 5k polys for a low poly chair is considered "acceptable" for a lot of games, I have several intense shaders that I've created in order to make my comic book style work, and they become exponentially more expensive with the number of polys they have to work with (as do shadows.) I'd rather be able to fit hundreds of thousands of objects on the screen at once with my 200 poly chairs than use some 5k poly chair with questionable UVs.

replies.author: arelath
replies.body:
As a game developer who's worked on AAA games for years, everyone in the AAA space is using GenAI to some degree right now and has been for the last couple years. For an example of a game with "primarily" AI generated visuals, look at Madden College Football. Do you really think they did 11,000 unique players and 150 stadiums by hand? No, they leaned heavily into GenAI. 

Here's why they "get away" with it and Indy studios don't:
1. Almost no asset is completely GenAI. An asset might have 20+ steps to get it game ready, often going through multiple artists hands. GenAI typically handles some/most of these steps to make the work go faster. It's typically not used as a complete asset generator. If GenAI doesn't work for some reason for a given step, the artist just steps in and does the work they would've had to do by hand a few years ago. 
2. AAA studios generally use GenAI not to save money, but to increase quality. For instance, animation uses GenAI extensively to make more realistic motion, especially when you take into account all the blending and transition animations permutations.
3. Studios have better and more specialized models, either licensed or built in house.
4. Like people hating on movie CGI, people don't actually hate CGI in movies, they hate BAD CGI in movies. We all do. Done well, CGI should be invisible and seamless. 
5. Good use of GenAI is invisible. Done correctly, typically in the hands of a skilled artist, you really can't tell the difference. AI looking parts are reworked, styles matched and in the end, the final assets are actually higher quality than something built without GenAI.
6. AAA games don't advertise their use of GenAI. 

By comparison, a lot of Indy developers are looking at GenAI to cut corners and it shows. If they're willing to ship absolute AI slop, I'm betting they cut corners everywhere and their game is also buggy and not a lot of fun to play (finding the fun is hard and takes a lot more time than you'd think).

replies.author: RuinoftheReckless
replies.body:
The thing i'm really curious about right now is the appetites of different 'genre fans' on Steam for AI art. 

In order to fairly evaluate that a 'genre of fans'; like Boomer Shooter FPS fans, or JRPG fans, survival horror fans... what you would want to see is several very high quality games in that genre that use primarily AI art that looks great and have either done well or not done well. 

If such games don't exist yet; there's no way to determine whether players of those games will be willing to buy games with AI assets. (poor quality AI games don't really help make that determination since nobody buys poor quality games of any kind.)

The example here is particularly interesting; because the art is not that great and obviously AI. So this shows that, if the gameplay is good, there are certainly at least some types of games that can succeed with obvious AI assets. B

The question that naturally follows is; how broad of a group is this, and does it cross genres? And we would need to see many more examples to establish a trend so it may just be too early to tell.  
  
So that's basically what i'm looking for right now. What are the trends on Steam? How do consumers, generally, feel about AI art, when it comes to spending their money on video games. If you have any other interesting examples I would be interested to see them too.

comments.author: Ben___Garrison

The closest I've seen isn't a full game released on Steam, but AI generated art mods for Slay the Spire have done unusually well. [This](https://www.nexusmods.com/slaythespire2/mods/344) is currently the 5th most downloaded, and the most-downloaded of any that isn't a simple utility pack. There are [plenty of others that have done well](https://www.nexusmods.com/games/slaythespire2/mods?tag=AI-Generated%20Content&tags_yes%5B%5D=4488) beyond that. 

Some people will *absolutely* react negatively if they know it's AI art, because they become hypersensitive to any perceived faults and specifically go out looking for issues that they would easily overlook if they thought it was human made. Here's [one blatant example](https://x.com/Jediwolf/status/2054776716770320631). Some big games are probably already using AI art extensively somewhere in the pipeline, but I doubt they'd admit to the full extent of it given the histrionic backlash it would be greeted with.

comments.author: ThePunisher2072
comments.body:
I started developing games right before AI game in. And when generative AI appeared it blew my mind. I was now capable of adding photorealistic graphics to my games without needing to sell my house or spending years just drawing things on my own. 

My passion was always creating, and I’ve been always decent at most art skills, but my tdah made it impossible to me to become a master in any art. But I’ve been always good at directing and managing projects or teams.

So finally this ai would help me create my visions completely and I started using it to create stories that could be moving for people.

The first project was a visual novel that relied a lot on video. And video generation was still too young, so I spent months doing tests, generating hundreds of takes for a simple couple of quick clips. Experimented with all known AIs, consistency was still a myth so I tried all sorts of ways to work, mixing with photoshop, retouching, but it was still too soon to build a phantasmagoria-like adventure and keep things as unneeded to be. Putting two characters in a single scene was almost a failure. 

Then I decided to put on Hold that project and started to work in another story my son had won a literature award a while ago, so he would find it attractive to work together. And I started it using AI despite I already knew there were people hating it. I thought it would become residual in a short time after lots of great games were released using ai. But it’s taking longer than expected.

In the meanwhile I’ve been working on a game that never tried to imitate anyone’s art style. I tried to do a kinda realistic style but using some design tips to make it coherent and cohesive. Thanks to AI, I was able to have digital actors without needing to pay and record actors. For months I created, refined, rebuilt, and did again thousands and thousands of graphics that later I fixed, refined and mastered in photoshop. I wanted to have realistic characters with alive expressions, and I experimented for months with all sorts of techniques. Finally when video became good as hell I found the way to put the characters in a virtual audition performing all sorts of poses so the. I could capture dozens of stills but making sure the character is always fully consistent, light coherent, and with no weird graphic issues. 

And in the meanwhile, we have worked night and day for 
Months. It’s become and obsession to me and I’ve spent more on this than I anything else in my entire life. Thanks to the AI I’ve been made to extend my original idea way way longer than I would have never believed. And the result, to me, is looking so great. We’ve created a pseudo 3d exploration engine, and we are creating lots of stories in every location that would have taken years if I had to do everything on my own. And I would have never looked so great. And I keep refining, rebuilding, and improving things to make it look consistent, coherent and cool. Recently I rebuilt dozens of old graphics that were outdated since the backgrounds were too random and I’ve been working on making sure the main location of the game is solid and coherent.

I have put so much time in everything. 

For the soundtrack I composed some simple Melodies on mY own (always was an amateur composer with fast tracker and reason) and then created literally thousands of variations with AI, trying different atmospheres, editing with studio, adding layers with logic audio, starting all over again, and again, and listening to dozens of tests every night, picking the best ones, and then remastering them and doing the best so they sound natural, cohesive and better than anything I could have produced just on my own.

And that’s the point. I could have created everything on my own, but in my look for quality, I believe I would have never been able to make it on my own because i would have created a minimal part of the assets I have now, everything would have looked cheap, and probably I would have lost interest with time. 

But now I’m struggling with hate every time I pay something with the game. Despite most people doesn’t mind about how the graphics were done, the realistic approach of the graphics can be spotted by AI haters, which consider doing realistic graphics was stealing. And it’s so sad to me because we’re putting so much effort into it, so much passion and heart that it breaks me to realize people will hate it just because I embraced the technology from the beginning and tried to extract all of its potential.

I’ve seen already youtube shorts and videos entirely done with ai that have been praised and loved because of the story and the coherence. And nobody cared anymore about the AI. AI Coding can’t be spotted if the game works. 3d AI can’t be spotted if done right. But hey, don’t try to generate any image with ai because that’s wrong.

It makes me really sad to know ow that my game is probably doomed. That probably nobody will play all those unique moments were creating to impact the player, to create a memorable experience and to enhance the survival narrative genre. 

I really expected our game to be ONE OF THOSE people said:”look, good games can be created thanks to AI. It depends on the heart behind it”.but now I know the game won’t have a chance after some haters destroy it as soon as they know about it, without even giving it a chance.

This is what I’ve managed to get after a few months of work. comments.author: Defiant_Bluejay_4549
comments.body:
A lot of indie games take years to finish. Even if someone started building a heavily AI-assisted game in 2024 or 2025, there’s a good chance it won’t be out for several more years.

So if you’re trying to judge whether AI-assisted game development works, only looking at released games seems a bit premature. A lot of the more ambitious projects are probably still being worked on.

The more interesting question is probably how many promising AI-assisted games are currently in development and haven’t shipped yet.
